text: A star spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. When the hydrogen runs low, the core contracts and heats while the outer layers swell, and a star like the Sun becomes a red giant before shedding its envelope.

The Moon always shows nearly the same face to Earth because its rotation period matches its orbital period. This tidal locking developed over a long time as gravitational friction slowed the Moon's spin until the two motions became synchronized.

Comets are loose bodies of ice and dust from the outer solar system. As one approaches the Sun, sunlight warms its surface, releasing gas and dust that form a glowing coma and a tail that always points away from the Sun.

Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has been observed for centuries. Its reddish color likely comes from chemicals in the upper atmosphere altered by sunlight, and the storm has slowly shrunk over recent decades.

Light from distant galaxies is stretched toward longer wavelengths as it travels through an expanding universe. Astronomers measure this redshift to estimate how far away a galaxy is and how long its light has been travelling toward us.

Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep underground, giving its crystals time to become large enough to see. The pale feldspar, glassy quartz, and dark mica flakes in a polished countertop record that long, gradual cooling.

Rivers carve canyons by carrying sand and pebbles that grind against the bedrock during floods. Over many thousands of years this abrasion, combined with slow uplift of the land, can cut gorges hundreds of meters deep.

Earthquakes occur when stress builds along a fault until the rocks suddenly slip. The energy released travels outward as seismic waves, and instruments on different continents record their arrival times to locate where the rupture began.

Limestone caves form as slightly acidic rainwater seeps through cracks and dissolves the rock. Where water drips into an open chamber, dissolved minerals are left behind, slowly building stalactites from the ceiling and stalagmites from the floor.

Glaciers move downhill under their own weight, plucking rocks from the valley floor and dragging them along. When the ice melts, it leaves behind U-shaped valleys, scattered boulders, and long ridges of mixed gravel called moraines.

Bread dough rises because yeast feeds on sugars and releases carbon dioxide. Kneading develops gluten strands that trap the gas, so a well-kneaded dough stretches thin without tearing and bakes into a light, open crumb.

Searing meat in a very hot pan creates a brown crust through the Maillard reaction, in which sugars and amino acids combine to form hundreds of flavorful compounds. Crowding the pan lowers the temperature and leaves the meat steamed and gray.

A good risotto depends on adding warm stock gradually while stirring. The friction releases starch from the surface of the rice, giving the dish a creamy texture even though very little cream or butter is added.

Egg whites whip into stiff peaks because beating unfolds their proteins, which then link around tiny air bubbles. A trace of yolk or grease interferes with this network, which is why bowls for meringue must be completely clean.

Pickling preserves vegetables by surrounding them with an acidic brine that keeps spoilage organisms from multiplying. Cucumbers left in salted water also ferment naturally as lactic acid bacteria gradually sour the liquid over several weeks.

Castles in the eleventh century were often simple wooden towers on earthen mounds surrounded by a ditch. Over the following centuries they were rebuilt in stone, with thicker walls, round towers, and gatehouses designed to withstand siege engines.

Medieval monasteries copied manuscripts by hand in rooms called scriptoria. Monks prepared parchment from animal skins, mixed inks from oak galls and iron salts, and sometimes spent months decorating a single page with gold leaf.

The Black Death reached Europe in the 1340s and killed a large share of the population within a few years. Labor shortages afterward weakened old obligations between peasants and lords in many regions.

Knights trained from childhood, first serving as pages in a noble household and later as squires who cared for armor and horses. Only after years of practice in riding and swordsmanship would a squire be formally dubbed a knight.

Pilgrims in the Middle Ages travelled long distances to shrines such as Santiago de Compostela. Along the routes, hostels and churches offered shelter, and travelers wore scallop shells as a sign of their journey.

Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light while reflecting green. In autumn, many trees stop making chlorophyll, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were present all along and adding red pigments as sugars accumulate.

Roots take up water partly through tiny hairs that greatly increase their surface area. Water then moves upward through narrow vessels in the stem, pulled by evaporation from pores in the leaves on warm, dry days.

Many flowers attract pollinators with color, scent, and nectar. Some orchids go further, mimicking the shape and odor of a female insect so that males attempt to mate with the flower and carry its pollen to the next bloom.
Seeds can remain dormant for years until conditions are right. Some require a period of cold, others need their hard coat scratched, and certain pine cones open only after the heat of a forest fire.

Plants bend toward a window because a hormone called auxin collects on the shaded side of the stem. Cells there elongate faster than those facing the light, so the stem curves gradually toward the brighter direction.

A major scale follows a fixed pattern of whole and half steps, which is why it sounds familiar whatever note it starts on. Changing the third, sixth, and seventh notes by a half step produces the darker natural minor scale.

Harmony in much Western music moves between tension and resolution. A dominant seventh chord contains a dissonant interval that pulls toward the tonic, and composers delay that resolution to build expectation in a phrase.

Time signatures tell performers how beats are grouped. A waltz in three-four time stresses the first of every three beats, while a march in two-four time alternates strong and weak beats in a steady left-right pattern.

Counterpoint combines independent melodies that sound coherent together. Composers in the Baroque period followed rules about parallel fifths and voice leading so that each line stayed distinct while the combined texture remained consonant.

The pitch of a vibrating string depends on its length, tension, and thickness. Halving the length of a string raises its pitch by an octave, a relationship that early theorists explored with simple instruments called monochords.

Thunderstorms form when warm, moist air rises rapidly into colder air above. As water vapor condenses, it releases heat that drives the updraft higher, and collisions between ice particles separate electrical charges that eventually discharge as lightning.

Fog is a cloud that forms at ground level. On clear nights the ground loses heat quickly, cooling the air just above it until moisture condenses into tiny droplets that linger in valleys until morning sunshine warms them.

Hurricanes draw their energy from warm ocean water. Air spiraling inward picks up moisture, and the heat released as that moisture condenses powers winds that can exceed two hundred kilometers per hour near the eye wall.

Snowflakes form as water vapor freezes directly onto tiny ice crystals high in a cloud. Temperature and humidity determine whether a crystal becomes a flat plate, a needle, or the familiar six-armed branching star.

A rainbow appears when sunlight enters falling raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of each drop, and bends again on the way out. Because each color bends by a slightly different amount, the light spreads into a curved band.

Gothic cathedrals used pointed arches and flying buttresses to carry the weight of tall stone vaults outward and down. This allowed builders to open the walls for large stained glass windows that filled the interior with colored light.

Roman engineers built the Pantheon's dome from concrete that became lighter toward the top, using pumice in the upper layers. A circular opening at the center reduces weight and lets a beam of sunlight move across the interior.

Traditional Japanese houses often used sliding paper screens instead of fixed walls. Rooms could be opened or divided as needed, and deep eaves shaded the interior in summer while letting in low winter sunlight.

Steel frames made skyscrapers possible because the walls no longer had to support the building's weight. Thin curtain walls of glass could hang from the frame, and elevators made the upper floors practical to reach.

Adobe buildings use thick walls of sun-dried mud brick that absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. In dry climates this keeps interiors cooler in the afternoon and warmer after dark.

In soccer, a player is offside if they are nearer to the opponent's goal line than both the ball and the second-to-last defender when the ball is played to them. Being offside is not an offence unless the player becomes involved in play.

A tennis game is scored with the unusual sequence of fifteen, thirty, forty, and game. If both players reach forty, the score is called deuce, and one player must then win two consecutive points to take the game.

In baseball, a batter receives a walk after four pitches outside the strike zone that they do not swing at. Three strikes result in an out, although a foul ball counts as a strike only until the batter has two.

Basketball teams must attempt a shot within a set number of seconds after gaining possession. The shot clock was introduced to stop teams from holding the ball for long stretches and to keep the pace of play moving.

In cricket, a bowler delivers six legal balls to make up an over, after which another bowler takes over from the opposite end. Wides and no-balls do not count toward the six and award an extra run to the batting side.

Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps that secrete limestone skeletons. Many corals depend on algae living inside their tissues, and when water becomes too warm the algae leave, causing the coral to turn white.

Octopuses can change the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second. Specialized cells containing pigment sacs expand or contract under nervous control, letting the animal blend into rocks, sand, or seaweed.

Humpback whales migrate thousands of kilometers between cold feeding waters and warm breeding areas. Males sing long, complex songs that change gradually from year to year and can be heard across great distances underwater.

Many deep-sea fish produce their own light through bioluminescence. Chemical reactions in special organs create a blue glow used to attract prey, find mates, or hide the fish's silhouette against faint light from above.

Sea turtles return to the beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. The temperature of the sand during incubation determines whether hatchlings become male or female, with warmer nests producing more females.
